messages.content:
She was wild to be at home--to hear, to see, to be upon the spot to share with Jane in the cares that must now fall wholly upon her, in a family so deranged; a father absent, a mother incapable of exertion, and requiring constant attendance; and though almost persuaded that nothing could be done for Lydia, her uncle's interference seemed of the utmost importance, and till he entered the room the misery of her impatience was severe. Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner had hurried back in alarm, supposing, by the servant's account, that their niece was taken suddenly ill; but satisfying them instantly on that head, she eagerly communicated the cause of their summons, reading the two letters aloud, and dwelling on the postscript of the last with trembling energy. Though Lydia had never been a favourite with them, Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner could not but be deeply affected. Not Lydia only, but all were concerned in it; and after the first exclamations of surprise and horror, Mr. Gardiner readily promised every assistance in his power. Elizabeth, though expecting no less, thanked him with tears of gratitude; and all three being actuated by one spirit, everything relating to their journey was speedily settled. They were to be off as soon as possible. "But what is to be done about Pemberley?" cried Mrs. Gardiner. "John told us Mr. Darcy was here when you sent for us;--was it so?"

Summarize this scene in three sentences.

Elizabeth is desperate to get home and help Jane after Lydia's elopement. When her aunt and uncle return, she reads them the letters, and Mr. Gardiner promises to help in every way. They plan to leave at once, and Mrs. Gardiner asks whether Darcy had been there.

Give me the gist of Heathcliff's speech, a sentence or two only.

"You suppose she has nearly forgotten me?" he said. "Oh, Nelly! you know she has not! You know as well as I do, that for every thought she spends on Linton she spends a thousand on me! At a most miserable period of my life, I had a notion of the kind: it haunted me on my return to the neighbourhood last summer; but only her own assurance could make me admit the horrible idea again. And then, Linton would be nothing, nor Hindley, nor all the dreams that ever I dreamt. Two words would comprehend my future—death and hell: existence, after losing her, would be hell. Yet I was a fool to fancy for a moment that she valued Edgar Linton's attachment more than mine. If he loved with all the powers of his puny being, he couldn't love as much in eighty years as I could in a day. And Catherine has a heart as deep as I have: the sea could be as readily contained in that horse-trough as her whole affection be monopolised by him. Tush! He is scarcely a degree dearer to her than her dog, or her horse. It is not in him to be loved like me: how can she love in him what he has not?"

Heathcliff insists that Catherine still thinks of him far more than of her husband. He says losing her would make life unbearable, and he scorns Edgar, claiming Edgar could never love her as deeply as he does.

What is Nana Kamal's message? Two sentences, please.

Arohi, you are still cross about Miss Fernandes, so listen to an old man. I am Kamal, your Nana. When I was ten, my teacher made me stand outside the class for a joke I had not made. I did not talk to her for a month. Then one day she stopped me in the corridor and said, "I was wrong to blame you. I am sorry." My eyes filled. I felt relief, but also a sore spot inside, like a scrape that had not healed. I nodded. Slowly I understood that teachers are people who slip too. When I forgave her, that weight left my chest.

Kamal tells his granddaughter that a teacher once punished him for a joke he did not make, and he stayed angry until she apologised. Forgiving her took time, but he learned that teachers make mistakes too, and letting go felt like a weight lifted.

Summarize this story in three short sentences.

In the small town of Sirsi, everyone knew when a family bought something new. When the Hegde family next door got a car, Deepak's mother mentioned it twice at dinner. When Sabina's colleague at the school went to Kerala for a holiday, the staff room talked about it for a week. So Deepak and Sabina bought a scooter on instalments, then a big fridge, then took a trip to Goa on the credit card. They never sat down to see if their two salaries, his at the cooperative bank and hers at the school, could carry it all. By the monsoon, the card bills were arriving faster than the salaries. They paid one card with another. The quarrels started small, about who had wanted the fridge. Then they happened almost every night. Their little son started going quiet whenever the phone rang. One evening Sabina sat on the step with the bills and simply cried.

Deepak and Sabina copied their neighbours' spending.
They bought a scooter, a fridge and a holiday on credit.
Soon the bills outgrew their pay, and they quarrelled every night.

How would you tell a child about this, in two simple sentences?

Natural philosophy is the genius that has regulated my fate; I desire, therefore, in this narration, to state those facts which led to my predilection for that science. When I was thirteen years of age we all went on a party of pleasure to the baths near Thonon; the inclemency of the weather obliged us to remain a day confined to the inn. In this house I chanced to find a volume of the works of Cornelius Agrippa. I opened it with apathy; the theory which he attempts to demonstrate and the wonderful facts which he relates soon changed this feeling into enthusiasm. A new light seemed to dawn upon my mind, and bounding with joy, I communicated my discovery to my father. My father looked carelessly at the title page of my book and said, "Ah! Cornelius Agrippa! My dear Victor, do not waste your time upon this; it is sad trash."
At thirteen, Victor found a book by Cornelius Agrippa on a day stuck indoors by bad weather and became very excited. Victor's father glanced at it and said not to waste time on it.

Please sum this text up in two sentences.

He was a man of about fifty, tall, portly, and imposing, with a massive, strongly marked face and a commanding figure. He was dressed in a sombre yet rich style, in black frock-coat, shining hat, neat brown gaiters, and well-cut pearl-grey trousers. Yet his actions were in absurd contrast to the dignity of his dress and features, for he was running hard, with occasional little springs, such as a weary man gives who is little accustomed to set any tax upon his legs. As he ran he jerked his hands up and down, waggled his head, and writhed his face into the most extraordinary contortions.
The man is about fifty, tall and dignified, in expensive dark clothes. But he is running hard, jerking his arms, shaking his head and making strange faces, which looks absurd.

Two sentences, please: what is this about?

A professional case of great gravity was engaging my own attention at the time, and the whole of next day I was busy at the bedside of the sufferer. It was not until close upon six o'clock that I found myself free and was able to spring into a hansom and drive to Baker Street, half afraid that I might be too late to assist at the denouement of the little mystery. I found Sherlock Holmes alone, however, half asleep, with his long, thin form curled up in the recesses of his armchair. A formidable array of bottles and test-tubes, with the pungent cleanly smell of hydrochloric acid, told me that he had spent his day in the chemical work which was so dear to him.

The narrator spends the day with a patient, then rushes to Baker Street at six, afraid of missing the end of the mystery. Holmes is found half asleep in an armchair among bottles and test-tubes after a day of chemistry.

Pick out the key points of this extract in two sentences.

And so she ran on, till I relinquished the endeavour to convince her of her mistake. She did not mention the visit that night, because she did not see Mr. Linton. Next day it all came out, sadly to my chagrin; and still I was not altogether sorry: I thought the burden of directing and warning would be more efficiently borne by him than me. But he was too timid in giving satisfactory reasons for his wish that she should shun connection with the household of the Heights, and Catherine liked good reasons for every restraint that harassed her petted will.

Catherine will not listen to the narrator's warning, and the next day the visit comes out. The narrator hopes Mr. Linton can rein Catherine in, but he is too timid to explain, and Catherine wants a reason for every rule.

Please sum this text up in three sentences.

When first Mr. Bennet had married, economy was held to be perfectly useless; for, of course, they were to have a son. This son was to join in cutting off the entail, as soon as he should be of age, and the widow and younger children would by that means be provided for. Five daughters successively entered the world, but yet the son was to come; and Mrs. Bennet, for many years after Lydia's birth, had been certain that he would. This event had at last been despaired of, but it was then too late to be saving. Mrs. Bennet had no turn for economy; and her husband's love of independence had alone prevented their exceeding their income.

When Mr. and Mrs. Bennet married, they did not save money because they expected a son who would help secure the family's future. Five daughters arrived instead, and by the time they gave up hope, it was too late to save. Mrs. Bennet was not careful with money, and only her husband's love of independence kept them within their income.

Shrink this to three sentences.

On Wednesday in the Chennai school library, Tanushree leaned over to Irawati and whispered, "Don't laugh, but I think I like Deepak." Irawati's pen froze. She'd liked Deepak since the inter-school quiz. She'd never told anyone. All evening in their flat, the jealousy grew. Deepak and Tanushree sat together in maths. What if he liked her back? Irawati found herself planning: she could mention to Deepak that Tanushree talks too much, or that she already has someone. She stopped. She pictured Tanushree's face if she ever found out. They had shared tiffins since Class 2. The next morning, before the bell, Irawati said, "Tanu, I should've told you yesterday. I like Deepak too." Tanushree blinked. "Oh. Oh no." "I'd rather lose the crush than lose you." Tanushree grabbed her hand. "Same. Let's not fight over a boy who doesn't even know we exist."

Tanushree whispers to Irawati that she likes Deepak, whom Irawati has secretly liked since the quiz. Irawati is jealous and thinks of saying unkind things about Tanushree, but stops, remembering their friendship. Next morning she tells Tanushree the truth, and they agree that their friendship matters more than a boy who does not know they exist.

What happens in this extract? Use two sentences.

"Come, there's no use in crying like that!" said Alice to herself, rather sharply; "I advise you to leave off this minute!" She generally gave herself very good advice, (though she very seldom followed it), and sometimes she scolded herself so severely as to bring tears into her eyes; and once she remembered trying to box her own ears for having cheated herself in a game of croquet she was playing against herself, for this curious child was very fond of pretending to be two people. "But it's no use now," thought poor Alice, "to pretend to be two people! Why, there's hardly enough of me left to make one respectable person!"

Alice sharply tells herself to stop crying, though she rarely follows her own good advice. She sadly sees that pretending to be two people is no use now, since there is hardly enough of her left to make one.

How would you explain this extract to a young child, in three sentences?

Our house was the house of mourning. My father's health was deeply shaken by the horror of the recent events. Elizabeth was sad and desponding; she no longer took delight in her ordinary occupations; all pleasure seemed to her sacrilege toward the dead; eternal woe and tears she then thought was the just tribute she should pay to innocence so blasted and destroyed. She was no longer that happy creature who in earlier youth wandered with me on the banks of the lake and talked with ecstasy of our future prospects. The first of those sorrows which are sent to wean us from the earth had visited her, and its dimming influence quenched her dearest smiles.

The narrator's home is full of sadness after the terrible events. The father's health is shaken, and Elizabeth is so sad that she takes no joy in her usual occupations. She is no longer the happy person who once walked by the lake with the narrator and talked about the future.

Tell me in three sentences what this section says.

"After all, Watson," said Holmes, reaching up his hand for his clay pipe, "I am not retained by the police to supply their deficiencies. If Horner were in danger it would be another thing; but this fellow will not appear against him, and the case must collapse. I suppose that I am commuting a felony, but it is just possible that I am saving a soul. This fellow will not go wrong again; he is too terribly frightened. Send him to gaol now, and you make him a gaol-bird for life. Besides, it is the season of forgiveness. Chance has put in our way a most singular and whimsical problem, and its solution is its own reward. If you will have the goodness to touch the bell, Doctor, we will begin another investigation, in which, also a bird will be the chief feature."

Holmes tells Watson he is not paid by the police to cover their gaps, so the case against Horner will collapse. He may be breaking the law but thinks he is saving a soul, as the man is too frightened to offend again. It is the season of forgiveness, so he asks Watson to ring the bell for the next case.

Sum up what happens in this excerpt using two sentences.

"'Bhishma said, "In this connection, O Yudhishthira, is cited the old story of the discourse between Amvarisha and Indra. Amvarisha, the son of Nabhaga, having repaired to heaven that is so difficult of acquisition, beheld his own generalissimo in those celestial regions in the company of Indra. The king saw his puissant general blazing with every kind of energy, endued with celestial form, seated on a very beautiful car, and journeying (in that vehicle) up and up towards still higher regions. Beholding the prosperity of his general Sudeva, and observing how he traversed regions that were still higher, the high-souled Amvarisha, filled with surprise, addressed Vasava, in the following words.

Bhishma tells Yudhishthira an old story about Amvarisha and Indra. Amvarisha reaches heaven and is surprised to see his general Sudeva with Indra, shining and riding a beautiful chariot to higher worlds.

"There is at least a presumption that the vessel in which the man or men are is a sailing-ship. It looks as if they always send their singular warning or token before them when starting upon their mission. You see how quickly the deed followed the sign when it came from Dundee. If they had come from Pondicherry in a steamer they would have arrived almost as soon as their letter. But, as a matter of fact, seven weeks elapsed. I think that those seven weeks represented the difference between the mail-boat which brought the letter and the sailing vessel which brought the writer."

Give this paragraph a two-sentence summary.

The speaker thinks the men are on a sailing ship, since they send their warning ahead of them. A steamer would have arrived about when the letter did, but seven weeks passed, the gap between a mail-boat and a sailing ship.

Capture this text in two sentences.

That was worse: she fretted and sighed, and looked at her watch till eight, and finally went to her room, completely overdone with sleep; judging by her peevish, heavy look, and the constant rubbing she inflicted on her eyes. The following night she seemed more impatient still; and on the third from recovering my company she complained of a headache, and left me. I thought her conduct odd; and having remained alone a long while, I resolved on going and inquiring whether she were better, and asking her to come and lie on the sofa, instead of upstairs in the dark. No Catherine could I discover upstairs, and none below. The servants affirmed they had not seen her. I listened at Mr. Edgar's door; all was silence. I returned to her apartment, extinguished my candle, and seated myself in the window.

Catherine grows restless, goes to her room early, then complains of a headache and leaves the narrator alone. When the narrator goes to check on her, she is nowhere to be found, and the servants say they have not seen her.

Break down this bit of text into three short sentences.

There was one district scholarship seat for their kasba school, and everyone knew it was between Jeevan and Zeenat. Jeevan couldn't stop thinking about her. He checked her test marks before his own, lay awake counting how many sums she'd done, and on the bus he watched her revise instead of revising himself. One afternoon he found her physics notebook left on a bench and held it a second too long, imagining it gone. His hands felt dirty. He put it back on her desk. That night he couldn't sleep again, and his mock-test score dropped by twelve marks. His grandfather, mending a net on the veranda, said, "You're running her race, not yours." Jeevan turned his desk to face the wall and made a timetable with no Zeenat in it.
Jeevan can think only of Zeenat, his rival for one scholarship seat. He holds her notebook too long, then puts it back. His grandfather says he is running her race, so he plans without her.

Describe this bit of text in just three sentences.

Pooja had led the milk collection team in the Anand district cooperative for a year. When she started, drivers and helpers quit every few months. She didn't give speeches. Instead, she learnt every person's name and something about their lives. Bhupen's daughter was writing her Class 10 boards. Kamla's husband had a bad knee. Each morning at the chilling centre, she asked about them. She also told them why the milk mattered: twelve villages, a school's midday meal, the co-op's tiny profits going back to farmers. Last month the private dairy offered Bhupen more money to drive for them. He said no. "Pooja-ben asks about my daughter's exams," he told the others. "Nobody else does." In her second year, not one person on the team left. Their collection times improved too.

Pooja has led a milk collection team in Anand for a year, and drivers and helpers used to quit every few months. She learns each person's name and life, asks about them each morning, and explains why the milk matters. Bhupen turns down a private dairy's offer of more money because Pooja asks about his daughter's exams, and in her second year nobody leaves.

The coffee machine on the fourth floor of the Copenhagen office had broken again, and when Emil walked into the small meeting room holding a mug of hot water, Layla laughed. "Brave choice." He laughed too. It helped; she had bad news. "The board turned down the recycling proposal," she said. "Not the idea itself. The budget, this year." Emil's smile went. He looked at the table. "I've put six months into it. Should I be worried about my job?" A reflex laugh rose in Layla's throat, the kind she used to soften things, and she swallowed it. This wasn't the moment. "No," she said steadily. "Your job isn't at risk. I'm sorry about the six months. I want to push it again next year, with you leading it." Emil breathed out. "Okay. Thank you for not laughing that off."

Please give me the main points of this paragraph in three sentences.

Layla tells Emil that the board turned down his recycling proposal for this year's budget, not the idea itself. Emil asks whether his job is at risk after six months of work, and Layla holds back a nervous laugh. She says his job is safe and wants to try again next year with him leading it.

Squeeze this conversation into under 60 words.

"Amma, Sharmila came to school with a new bag today. Purple, with a unicorn zip." "Nice. First day after the summer holidays, everyone wants something new." "She's showing off. She kept putting it on the desk so everyone could see." "Where else would she put it?" "She's jealous of everyone, Amma. That's why she needs fancy things." "Who is she jealous of?" "Everyone! She looked at my water bottle." Amma glanced at Pooja's old blue bag, its strap tied in a knot. "Did you like the purple one?" "No." Pooja kicked the bag under the table. "Unicorns are for babies." She was quiet for a moment. "Can mine get fixed before the rains?"
Pooja complains that Sharmila is showing off a new purple unicorn bag. Amma asks if she liked it; Pooja says no, then asks if her own old bag can be fixed before the rains.
